newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Rabuka says Fiji reform may mean compulsory voting.
newsitem.headline: Rabuka says Fiji reform may mean compulsory voting.

text.p: Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, in New Zealand on Friday, predicted compulsory registration of voters and compulsory voting rules would be considered in plans for constitutional reform.

Just over 10 years ago Rabuka was the military commander at the head of a bloodless coup, and kidnapped the then Indian-dominated government, in a move intended to prevent indigenous Fijians losing control of their country to Indian Fijians.

He told Radio New Zealand on Friday that under the proposed new multi-party constitution it would be possible for Fiji's Indians to win a majority, especially as it was likely that the turnout would be greater from the minority community.
Indian Fijians make up about 46 percent of the islands' 750,000 population. Indians were brought to Fiji at the turn of the century to work on the country's sugar cane plantations.
Asked if there could be an Indian majority election result, Rabuka said, "Theoretically, yes."

"In fact, that is the main worry from the Fijians, who are worried about the boundaries of open seats, with the big concentration of Indians around the urban (areas) and sugar cane belt, that they could, in fact, win the majority of those seats in those areas," he said.
Indigenous Fijians were also concerned at "the trend that more Indians will register as voters and of those that register more Indians will go to vote," he added.
"We are right now looking at the question of compulsory registration and voting," Rabuka went on.
Asked if this would be brought in after ratification of the constitution he said: "Not necessarily after, we are looking at it now".

The issue had been raised at meetings of the Joint Parliamentary Select Committee, that designed the constitutional reform package over the last eight months, which were continuing after requests from the Council of Chiefs and others, he said.
Rabuka described the Great Council of Chiefs as the supreme council of the indigenous Fijian people.
Against the background of these moves, Rabuka said he remained confident that Fiji could be re-admitted to the Commonwealth, from which it was ejected after the 1987 coup.
Asked if he thought it likely the organisation would invite his country back he said: "Yes, hopefully they will do that."
The premier said he agreed the 10 years since the coup had been costly in terms of economic progress, but saw the approach as justified because it averted "a very bad racial situation".

"I believe it is worth it because we can come back from the brink of (what) we were facing in 1987, from the economic problems we've had in the following 10 years -- I believe we can still make a big turnaround."
At a later address to New Zealand businessmen in Waitangi, in the North Island, he said he wanted to assure potential and existing investors that reforms were firmly on track.
He said they could be sure they were dealing with a "multi-racial and multi-cultural country that it committed to consolidating and reinforcing its oneness and its unity as a nation".
